summary: Protocols that use Unicode in strings such as usernames and identifiers must handle them consistently, including when comparing them. This document defines the PRECIS framework, which specifies how to prepare, enforce rules on and compare internationalized strings across application protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: When a protocol carries a name that may contain letters from any writing system, two sides must agree on which characters are allowed and on how to decide that two names are the same. PRECIS is the rulebook for that. It defines two classes of allowed characters and a way for each protocol to add its own rules, such as turning capital letters into small ones before comparing.

subtitle: A framework for preparing, checking and comparing text strings that contain letters outside the ASCII range.

tldr.problem: Application protocols that put text in usernames, room names and other slots have to decide which characters are allowed and how two strings are judged to be the same. The old Stringprep framework was tied to an old version of Unicode and had to be abandoned for domain names.
tldr.mechanism: PRECIS defines two string classes, IdentifierClass and FreeformClass, that say which Unicode code points are valid, contextually allowed, disallowed or unassigned, and a set of profiles that add width mapping, case mapping, normalization and directionality rules.
tldr.outcome: This document replaced RFC 7564, which had defined an earlier version of the framework, and registers the string classes, the profiles and the derived property table with IANA.

today: RFC 8264 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 7564, an earlier version of the same framework. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Another String Framework
sections.content:
Application protocols that use Unicode code points in protocol strings have to handle those strings properly, both to enforce internationalization rules for the strings placed in various protocol slots, such as addresses and identifiers, and to perform valid comparison operations, for example for authentication or authorization. This document defines a framework that lets application protocols do that preparation, enforcement and comparison of internationalized strings in a way that depends on the properties of Unicode code points, and is therefore more agile with respect to versions of Unicode. PRECIS is restricted to Unicode and does not support any other coded character set.

Many IETF protocols had used the Stringprep framework as the basis for preparing, enforcing and comparing protocol strings containing Unicode code points. Stringprep was developed during work on internationalized domain names, and Nameprep was the Stringprep profile for those names. It was designed as a general framework so that other application protocols could define their own profiles, and a number of them did.

After Stringprep was published in 2002, significant issues arose with its use for internationalized domain names, most significantly that it was tied to Unicode version 3.2. The newer IDNA specifications, called IDNA2008, no longer use Stringprep and Nameprep. That migration prompted other users of Stringprep to look for new approaches.

This document defines a framework on four principles: a small set of string classes that specify the code points appropriate for common application-protocol constructs, where possible keeping compatibility with IDNA2008; definitions of each class in terms of code point properties, so an algorithm can decide whether each code point is valid, allowed in certain contexts, disallowed or unassigned; an inclusion model, so a class consists only of code points that are explicitly allowed and anything not explicitly allowed is forbidden; and profiles that let application protocols adjust the behaviour that matters, such as width mapping, case mapping, normalization and directionality, while strongly discouraging the multiplication of profiles beyond necessity.

The document stresses that the transformation of an input string to an output string is rarely reversible: case mapping would turn an input string of StPeter into stpeter, losing the capitalization of the first and third characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols that carry names need one shared answer to two questions: which characters are allowed, and when are two names the same. The earlier rules were tied to an old version of Unicode and had to be dropped for domain names, so the IETF defined a new framework for the other protocols to use.

sections.title: Preparation, Enforcement and Comparison
sections.content:
The document distinguishes three actions an entity can take with a string. Enforcement means applying all the rules of a string class, or a profile of it, to a single input string to check whether the string conforms and therefore whether it can be used in a given protocol slot. Comparison means applying the same rules to two separate input strings to determine whether they are equivalent. Preparation mainly means ensuring that the code points in an input string are allowed by the underlying string class, and sometimes applying one or more of the rules of a class or profile. Preparation suits constrained devices that can restrict the characters they offer a user but lack the processing power or memory for operations such as Unicode normalization. It does not ensure that the input string conforms to all the rules.

In most cases, authoritative entities such as servers are responsible for enforcement, while subsidiary entities such as clients are responsible only for preparation. The rationale is that clients may lack the memory and processing power to enforce all the rules, although they can more easily limit the characters they offer a user, and a server acts as the authority on acceptable strings in slots such as addresses and endpoint identifiers. A client also cannot necessarily be trusted to generate such strings properly, especially for security-sensitive contexts such as authentication and authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Three jobs are kept apart. Enforcement checks one string against the rules. Comparison checks two strings against each other. Preparation is a light pre-check that a small device can do. Servers do the enforcement; clients usually only prepare.

sections.title: The Two String Classes
sections.content:
The community weighed the cost of a small set of code points, which reduces the confusion caused by visually similar characters and makes a class relatively safe, against a much larger set, which allows more creativity and makes a class relatively expressive. It concluded that most existing uses could be addressed by two classes.

The IdentifierClass is a sequence of letters, numbers and some symbols used to identify or address a network entity, such as a user account, a chat room, a data feed or a file. The intent is to minimize user confusion, so safety has been prioritized over expressiveness. Its valid code points are the LetterDigits category, and the printable ASCII range from U+0021 to U+007E, which are grandfathered in even where the property-based rules would disallow them. A number of exception code points and the joining code points are allowed only when a contextual rule is met. Old Hangul Jamo, control code points, ignorable code points, space code points, symbol code points and punctuation code points are disallowed, as are code points that decompose and recompose into something other than themselves under Unicode Normalization Form KC, and letters and digits other than the traditional ones allowed in internationalized domain names. Code points not yet designated in Unicode are treated as disallowed.

The FreeformClass is a sequence of letters, numbers, symbols, spaces and other code points used for free-form strings, including passwords and human-friendly nicknames. The intent is to allow nearly any Unicode code point, so expressiveness has been prioritized over safety, and the document carries a security warning about it. Spaces, symbols and punctuation are valid here, as are code points with compatibility equivalents and the other letters and digits. Old Hangul Jamo, control code points and ignorable code points are disallowed, and unassigned code points are again treated as disallowed.

The IdentifierClass range is wider than the one allowed in IDNA2008, because IDNA2008 applies the Unstable category before the LetterDigits category and so disallows uppercase code points, while the IdentifierClass does not apply the Unstable category.
sections.plainLanguage: The strict class is for names that identify something: user accounts, chat rooms, file names. It allows letters, digits and most printable ASCII characters, but not spaces, symbols or punctuation. The loose class is for free text such as passwords and nicknames, and allows almost anything except control characters.

sections.title: Profiles and Their Rules
sections.content:
A profile of a PRECIS string class must define the width mapping, additional mapping, case mapping, normalization and directionality rules. It may also restrict the allowable code points further, but must not add any code point that the class disallows. Profile names take the form Profilename of BaseClass, so the profile for opaque strings such as passwords is the OpaqueString profile of the FreeformClass.

The width mapping rule says whether fullwidth and halfwidth code points are mapped to their decomposition mappings, so that, for example, the fullwidth digit zero maps to the ordinary digit zero. Because width mapping happens as part of compatibility decomposition, a profile using Normalization Form KD or KC does not need to specify it; a profile using Normalization Form C, which is recommended, does, and width mapping is generally recommended there.

The additional mapping rule says whether extra mappings are performed, such as mapping delimiter code points, or mapping special code points such as non-ASCII spaces to the ordinary space or control code points to nothing. The case mapping rule says whether uppercase and titlecase code points are mapped to their lowercase equivalents. The Unicode toLowerCase() operation is recommended over toCaseFold(), because it is less likely to surprise users. Mapping to lowercase is not recommended for FreeformClass strings used as passwords; instead the case should be preserved and compared case-sensitively.

The normalization rule says which of the four Unicode normalization forms is applied. Normalization Form C is recommended, and the document warns that NFKC and NFKD can lose a lot of information, in ways that depend on the language and script of the strings.

The directionality rule says how strings containing right-to-left code points are treated. A string that mixes right-to-left and left-to-right code points is bidirectional, and the same string can be displayed differently in interfaces configured for different scripts. The document defines no new directionality rules and strongly suggests profile authors use the Bidi Rule of IDNA2008 for IdentifierClass profiles, or the Unicode bidirectional algorithm for FreeformClass profiles.

The document also warns against multiplying profiles. Too many profiles make behaviour differ across applications, which violates what user interface design calls the Principle of Least Astonishment, and the document acknowledges that there are already too many.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile adds the decisions that matter for one protocol: whether to fold wide characters into narrow ones, whether to change capital letters to small ones, which Unicode form to normalize to, and how to treat text written right to left. The document strongly discourages every protocol from inventing its own profile, because too many profiles make the same name behave differently in different applications.

sections.title: The Order of Operations
sections.content:
To ensure proper comparison, the rules of a string class or profile must be applied in this order: the width mapping rule, the additional mapping rule, the case mapping rule, the normalization rule, the directionality rule, and finally the behavioural rules that decide whether a code point is valid, allowed under a contextual rule, disallowed or unassigned. The first five are set by each profile; the behavioural rules are set by each string class. The order matches IDNA2008, and Stringprep before it, so that code can be reused and there is as much continuity as possible with the Stringprep profiles that several PRECIS profiles obsolete.

Because of this order, applying the rules is not necessarily idempotent. For example, under Normalization Form KC, normalizing after case mapping can still yield uppercase characters for certain code points. An implementation should therefore apply the rules repeatedly until the output string is stable. If the output does not stabilize after three further applications following the first, the implementation should stop and reject the input string as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: The steps have to run in one fixed order, or two strings could compare differently depending on which order was used. Because some steps can undo earlier ones, the steps are repeated until the string stops changing, and the string is rejected if it still will not settle after four attempts in total.

sections.title: How Applications Should Use PRECIS
sections.content:
The document warns that internationalization does not become easy through PRECIS, and that the safest option for many protocol slots is still to support only the ASCII range. When a developer does support internationalized strings, the document gives guidance. Do not define a new profile unless absolutely necessary, because existing profiles are designed for wide reuse and an existing one will very likely fit. Do specify exactly which entities are responsible for preparation, enforcement and comparison, such as servers or clients; exactly when those entities need to complete their tasks; and exactly which protocol slots are checked against which profiles, for example checking the recipient address of a message against the UsernameCaseMapped profile of the IdentifierClass, or checking a user's password against the OpaqueString profile of the FreeformClass.

An application protocol may also exclude further code points, either specific ones that the class allows or ones matching certain Unicode properties, such as math symbols. Such exclusions are usually for backward compatibility with legacy formats, and are defined by the application protocol rather than by a profile, so that profiles are not multiplied.

Some application-layer constructs do not map neatly to a string class. The simple username in SASL might take the form of a person's full name with a space in it, which cannot be an IdentifierClass instance because spaces are not allowed there. It can instead be defined as a space-separated sequence of IdentifierClass instances, with the ABNF username = userpart *(1*SP userpart) and userpart = 1*(idpoint). The same technique can define constructs such as user@domain or /path/to/file.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a profile that already exists if one fits. Say plainly which side checks the string and which slot is checked. If a name needs a space in it, build it from several identifier-like pieces separated by spaces instead of inventing a new class.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If strings that look the same to users are treated as different by one system and the same by another, or the other way round, users become confused, and that confusion can have security consequences such as the false accepts and false rejects described in RFC 6943. One starting goal of the PRECIS work was to limit how often users are confused, which has proved difficult given the number of application protocols already in existence. Profiles should still not be multiplied, and protocol designers should think hard before defining a new one.

Applications depend on the correct preparation, enforcement and comparison of internationalized strings, since such strings can drive authentication and authorization decisions, and security can be compromised if an entity providing a string is connected to the wrong account because two systems read the string differently.

Strings conforming to the IdentifierClass are relatively safe because they include only letters, digits and grandfathered non-space ASCII code points, so they exclude spaces, code points with compatibility equivalents, and almost all symbols and punctuation. They can still include confusable code points. Strings conforming to the FreeformClass can include virtually any Unicode code point, which is expressive but problematic for user confusion; designers are encouraged to profile the IdentifierClass wherever feasible, and where more code points are needed to define a profile of the FreeformClass that restricts them as tightly as possible.

Confusable characters are not only a problem outside ASCII: the string ju1iet with a digit one can look like juliet, a phenomenon sometimes called typejacking. Outside ASCII it is worse, with, for example, the Cyrillic small letter a and the Latin small letter a easily mistaken for one another.

For passwords, the two goals are to maximize entropy and to minimize false accepts. It is therefore not recommended to profile the FreeformClass in a way that removes whole categories, such as by disallowing symbols or punctuation, and not recommended to map uppercase and titlecase code points to lowercase; the case should be preserved and compared in a case-sensitive way. Where a password is fed into a cryptographic algorithm, the client must prepare it properly, because the server never sees it in cleartext.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole point of the framework is to stop two systems disagreeing about whether two names are the same, because that disagreement can let one person log in as another. The strict class is the safer one, but even it can contain characters that look alike. Passwords need special care: keep their case, and do not strip out whole categories of characters, because that reduces how hard they are to guess.

sections.title: Interoperability Considerations
sections.content:
Some existing applications and systems do not support the full Unicode coded character set, or even any characters outside the ASCII repertoire. If two systems need to interoperate while exchanging data, they need at least one coded character set and one repertoire of characters in common. Establishing that baseline is a matter for the application that uses PRECIS, not for the framework. Unicode is the only coded character set PRECIS supports, so the rules cannot be applied to a system that does not support Unicode. The exact encoding is also a matter for the application protocol: strings are often encoded in UTF-8, but the framework does not require it.

It is important to understand that changes across Unicode versions can cause instability in the PRECIS categories. Between Unicode 5.2 and Unicode 6.0, three code points changed their GeneralCategory, which led to different handling depending on which version a system had. The HasCompat categorization of a string can change if the string includes a precomposed character added in a recent version of Unicode, and the East Asian width property used in many width mapping rules is not guaranteed to be stable across versions.

The document also records that, at the time of writing, issues raised during the review of Unicode 7.0 for IDNA had not been settled, and that the specification is likely to be updated. One possible change is that the range of code points in the LetterDigits category might be narrowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two programs that use PRECIS still have to agree on a character set, and usually that means Unicode. Because Unicode itself changes between versions, a character can be classified differently in one release than in another, so the framework publishes a table of classifications for each Unicode version.

items.title: Width mapping
items.text: Whether fullwidth and halfwidth code points are mapped to their ordinary forms.

items.title: Additional mapping
items.text: Whether delimiters and special code points are mapped, for example to a space or to nothing.

items.title: Case mapping
items.text: Whether uppercase and titlecase code points become lowercase. The Unicode toLowerCase() operation is recommended.

items.title: Normalization
items.text: Which of the four Unicode normalization forms is applied. Form C is recommended.

items.title: Directionality
items.text: How strings that mix right-to-left and left-to-right text are treated.
